items.label: What would better-supported rest make possible?

items.text: Sleep supports how we feel and function. Helpful habits include a fairly regular sleep schedule, a quieter wind-down, daylight and suitable activity during the day, and a dark, quiet sleeping space. Caffeine later in the day and alcohol near bedtime can interfere with sleep.
Shift work, caring, pain and health conditions can change what is realistic. Choose an action within your influence. You cannot command yourself to fall asleep.
Notice the opportunity

items.label: What would I like food to support in my life?

items.text: Food gives us energy and nutrients. It can also hold pleasure, culture, comfort, routine and connection. Calories describe energy; they do not describe the whole nutritional value or meaning of a meal.
Protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals, hydration and enough food all matter. So do access, appetite, allergies and medical needs. A choice that is useful for someone else may be unsuitable for you.

items.text: Protein can support fullness. Fibre, food volume, flavour, texture and eating enough also matter. A meal that suits one person may leave another hungry. Notice your pattern across a few ordinary meals before making a sweeping conclusion.

In a small controlled study, 20 adults ate freely from an ultra-processed menu and an unprocessed menu for two weeks each. They ate about 500 more calories a day on the ultra-processed menu, gaining an average 0.9 kg while losing 0.9 kg on the other menu. The gain was not all fat. This study compared whole menus; it did not test the brands in this journal or predict an individual result.
Try looking at the whole meal

At home or with a takeaway, consider the food you enjoy, a protein source, available vegetables and portions that fit your appetite and circumstances. Sauces, sides and drinks are part of the meal too. Convenience foods can be useful; processing alone is not a complete guide to nutritional value.

items.text: Your body uses energy to keep you alive, digest food and do everyday activities. Over time, the relationship between intake and expenditure influences body weight. It is not a simple explanation of your health, habits or worth.
Pattern over time
What it means

items.text: Estimates are starting points. Energy needs vary, food records have errors and requirements can change. Weight change also includes water and other tissues, so short-term scale changes do not measure fat change precisely.

items.text: Weight loss is not needed to use the body-check or reflection chapters. Muscle, energy, comfort, food enjoyment and everyday function can matter regardless of weight change.
1 / Estimate resting energy
The Mifflin-St Jeor equation uses weight in kilograms, height in centimetres and age in years. It estimates resting energy; this is not a daily food target.
(10 × kg) + (6.25 × cm) − (5 × age) Then -161 for the original female equation, or +5 for the original male equation.
Example: 75 kg, 170 cm, age 40.
Female equation: 1,451.5 kcal/day. Male equation: 1,617.5 kcal/day.

For adults aged 18+; not for pregnancy or breastfeeding. A result is not a prescription. Read Choose your approach · p. 19 for other reasons to seek individual advice first.

For adults for whom fat loss is appropriate, a modest adjustment may be more manageable than a large cut. A practical starting example is 10-20% below an estimated maintenance level, often towards 10-15% first. Review wellbeing and a longer-term pattern before changing it.
Example goal At 2,000 kcal maintenance
10-20% deficit 1,600-1,800 kcal/day
Maintenance About 2,000 kcal/day
5-10% surplus 2,100-2,200 kcal/day
A surplus is sometimes used alongside resistance training for muscle gain; it is not a recommendation that everyone should eat more. This workbook does not prescribe a training programme.
Arithmetic: a 15% deficit uses maintenance × 0.85: 2,000 × 0.85 = 1,700. Maintenance uses 1.00; a 5% surplus uses 1.05.

items.text: Protein supplies building blocks for body tissues. Adequate protein and appropriate resistance training can help preserve muscle during weight loss. Protein does not replace enough food overall, and powders are optional.
Context Daily guide
Basic adult reference 0.83 g per kg body weight
Healthy older adults, usually 65+ 1.0-1.2 g/kg
Healthy adults exercising regularly 1.4-2.0 g/kg

These describe different contexts; do not add them together. A higher-end figure sometimes used with resistance training is 1 g per pound, about 2.2 g/kg. It is not a minimum everyone needs. Many people do well with less.
Example: 75 kg × 1.6 = 120 g/day. At 2.2 g/kg, the same weight gives 165 g/day. Count protein from all foods, and keep fruit, vegetables, fibre, carbohydrates and suitable fats in the picture.

title: What the scales can tell me

items.text: Body weight includes fat, muscle, water, bones, organs and the contents of your digestive system. A change on the scales cannot tell you which part changed. Salt, stored carbohydrate, menstrual-cycle changes, meals, drinks and the timing of a reading can affect the number.
500 ml of water weighs about 0.5 kg That is the weight of the water, not body fat. Keep drinking normally. A weigh-in is never a reason to restrict fluids.
Home body-fat scales estimate body composition. Do not treat a daily “fat gained” or “muscle lost” message as a precise finding. Scale weight also cannot tell you how strong, fit or healthy you are.
When it helps
When it takes over
It answers a useful question about a longer-term trend without deciding the rest of your day.
You repeatedly check, feel judged by the reading, skip food or change your day to compensate.

items.label: What would I want weighing to help me understand?
My choice: use the scales / take a break / no home weighing. Why?

items.text: Follow an existing healthcare monitoring plan. For under-18s, pregnancy or an eating-disorder history, seek individual advice rather than planning weight change alone.

Use the same scales on a firm, level floor, at a similar time and in similar clothing. Morning after the toilet and before breakfast is one practical option. Ask for an accessible alternative if standing is difficult.

Weekly is a simple choice. Daily readings are optional if they feel neutral and you use an average; less often or no weighing is fine. Do not weigh more than once a day unless your care team advises it. Keep food and fluids normal.

items.text: If using several readings

Add them, then divide by how many you recorded. Example: 75.0 + 75.4 + 74.8 + 75.2 = 300.4 kg. Divide by 4 = 75.1 kg. A later set of 74.9, 74.5, 74.8 and 75.4 averages 74.9 kg: the final reading rose, but the average fell.

These are example numbers, not target weights. Keep units, timing and frequency similar when comparing averages. Include higher readings too. Look across several weeks; even a trend does not precisely measure fat change.

items.text: A total number of hours cannot tell you the whole story. Look at what you do, when you do it, how it leaves you feeling and what it may replace: sleep, movement, concentration or being with someone.
Ask about the experience as well as the hours. After using this app, do I feel connected, informed, rested, distracted, tense or something else?

In a 2025 randomised trial, blocking mobile internet on phones for two weeks improved measured attention, wellbeing and mental-health outcomes. Calls, texts and internet on other devices remained available. This was a specific intervention, with adherence limits; it does not establish a universal daily screen-time limit or prove that a particular device will help you.

items.text: Meditation includes practices that train attention or awareness. Mindfulness-based approaches may help some people with stress and other symptoms, but results vary and research has limitations. You do not have to feel calm afterwards for your observation to be useful.

items.text: Use stable equipment, a clear non-slip space, suitable footwear and any usual walking aid. Have a helper where the method asks for one. Warm up briefly with comfortable familiar movement; rest between checks until recovered. Avoid testing when unwell or unusually fatigued.

Stop rather than push through Stop for pain, dizziness, loss of control or feeling unwell. Chest pain, fainting, severe unusual breathlessness or new weakness need urgent medical help. In Ireland, call 112 or 999; elsewhere use your local emergency number.

Get individual advice first after recent surgery or injury, unexplained fainting, repeated falls, or with a condition that affects safe activity. If balance is uncertain, work with a qualified professional. Never arrange an unsupported challenge simply to obtain a score.

items.text: Effort scale used here: 0 = resting; 10 = maximum effort. It describes your experience, not a target to reach. These adult reference tables do not apply to children.
You need: a firm armless chair against a wall, a timer and a helper to count. The standard setup uses a seat about 43 cm / 17 inches high. Measure and record the height.
1. Sit in the middle of the seat, feet flat, back upright. Cross your wrists and place your
hands on opposite shoulders, arms against your chest.
2. On “Go”, stand fully, then sit back down under control. Continue for 30 seconds.
3. Count full stands. Count the final rise if you are more than halfway up when time ends.
Practise two rises, then rest at least a minute and until recovered before one recorded attempt. Stop if control is lost or symptoms appear. Keep the practice and rest routine the same next time.

If you need your hands Stop the standard test and record 0 under that test’s scoring rule. After resting, an assisted version may use a firm armchair or fixed support. Record that support and keep the assisted result separate.

Mark two lines 1 metre apart on a clear, non-slip floor. Practise both directions. On “Go”, side-step from one line to the other without crossing your feet. Optional cue task / 10 instructions

With a helper, mark a target about 30 cm to each side of a centre point. The helper gives 10 “left” or “right” cues, 5 of each, in a newly mixed order, around 4 seconds apart. Step to the named target and return to centre. Record correct responses and balance errors. Stop if unsteady or unable to return before the next cue without rushing. Hearing, understanding and practice can affect this task; it is not a laboratory reaction-time test.

Seated alternative: tap left and right targets on a table to the same cue pattern, using a comfortable reach. Label and compare this separately. Supported side-stepping along a fixed counter can instead be observed without timing speed.

items.text: Return to the daily check-in (p. 2) or weekly reflection (p. 6) when useful. If you already keep a separate tracker, there is no need to copy its daily figures here.
Food guidance WHO: Healthy diet; NICE NG246: Physical activity and diet. General guidance; the percentage adjustments here are planning examples, not a universal NICE target.

Energy estimates Mifflin et al. (1990), resting-energy equation, AJCN, 51, 241-247 (PMID 2305711). Activity factors are simplified estimates. NIDDK Body Weight Planner offers an alternative calculation.

Fullness and food intake Hall et al. (2019), ultra-processed versus unprocessed menus, Cell Metabolism, 30, 67-77.e3. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008. The small, short trial compared whole diets, not individual brands.

Protein reference amounts EFSA (2012): adult protein reference values; Bauer et al. (2013), PROT-AGE (doi:10.1016/j.jamda.2013.05.021); Jäger et al. (2017), ISSN position stand (doi:10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8); Morton et al. (2018), resistance-training review (PMID 28698222). These concern different populations and purposes.
Energy used in processing nutrients National Academies (2023), Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, chapter 6, drawing on Westerterp (2004). Do not subtract these percentages from a food log.

Product examples Label sources: Brennans Be Good Wholemeal and Family Pan; Arla Skyr Natural; Glenisk Organic Greek Style Natural; Tesco Roast Chicken Breast Pieces and Breaded Chicken Goujons; Flora Lighter; Lurpak Slightly Salted. Values are illustrations: check the current pack and the preparation method.
Optional logging help MyFitnessPal: How to log food to your diary explains the app steps if you choose to use it. Food notes without numbers are also useful.
Established test methods CDC STEADI assessment sheets: 30-second chair stand, four-stage balance and Timed Up and Go. Match the written setup when interpreting a result.

Chair-stand reference figures Jones, Rikli & Beam (1999), chair-stand study (PMID 10380242); Jones & Rikli (2002), Measuring functional fitness of older adults; Suetta et al. (2019), Copenhagen Sarcopenia Study (doi:10.1002/jcsm.12477). The younger-adult figures use a different chair and completion rule.

Mobility methods Jones et al. (1998), chair sit-and-reach (PMID 9864752); Powden et al. (2015), weight-bearing lunge reliability (PMID 25704110). Neither provides a universal pass/fail score for every home movement check.

Adaptations and demonstrations The adapted activities are observations, not a validated clinical assessment. Demonstration links stay beside each activity; follow this journal’s written timing and scoring where a video differs.

Sleep and meditation evidence NHLBI: Healthy sleep habits; NCCIH: Meditation and mindfulness - effectiveness and safety. The brief pause in this journal is an original practice invitation, not a tested treatment protocol.

Screen-time study Castelo et al. (2025), blocking mobile internet, PNAS Nexus, 4, pgaf017. doi:10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf017. This two-week trial does not establish a universal safe screen-time limit or test the Brick product.
Step-count setup: Apple Health and Google Fit official help are linked with QR codes on p. 7. Step counts are estimates; a description of movement is an alternative.

GROW model credit Whitmore, J. (2017), Coaching for Performance, 5th ed., Nicholas Brealey. GROW is associated with Whitmore and colleagues; the wording here is original. The Wheel of Life is a separate reflection tool.

Weighing: usefulness and emotional effects Madigan et al. (2015), systematic review (PMCID PMC4546162); 2016 correction: 10.1186/s12966-016-0366-x. Steinberg et al. (2014), adult trial (PMCID PMC4157390); Pacanowski et al. (2015), young-person observational study (PMID 26566095). Different populations and methods; weighing remains optional.

Interpreting weight and body-composition readings Hall et al. (2011), energy imbalance and body weight (PMCID PMC3880593); Kanellakis et al. (2023), menstrual-cycle changes (PMID 37395124); Frija-Masson et al. (2021), smart-scale accuracy (doi:10.2196/22487).
Optional practical guidance NHS England: How to record your weight explains a consistent weighing setup if tracking serves a useful purpose for you.
A few useful extras
The links and QR codes sit beside the relevant chapters.
Sleep / The Matt Walker Podcast The linked episode offers more detail on deep sleep for readers who want to explore the topic.
Meditation / davidji The linked five-minute recording offers a voice to follow when you would prefer guidance.
Attention / Brick An optional device and app to explore if you want a physical step between yourself and selected apps. Free built-in controls are also options.
